Across three models (1.5B–8B) and three regimes (needle retrieval, long chain-of-thought, and multi-turn recall), we measure head behavior on four model-regime combinations and find that most heads change their reading behavior at least once during generation. We introduce WakeKV , a reactive residency policy that moves cooling heads to a recoverable CPU reservoir rather than freezing or permanently evicting their state. At matched memory or budget, WakeKV consistently improves miss rate over frozen classification and destructive eviction—evaluated across five model-regime combinations—and over three cited baselines (SnapKV, uniform R-KV, and ReasonAlloc) across four eligible combinations. A FlexiCache/vLLM implementation on Mistral-7B confirms the benefit on real hardware, improving throughput while retaining LongBench quality. 1 Introduction KV-cache size dominates long-context LLM serving memory: caching every attended key/value pair for every head grows linearly in sequence length and quickly exceeds GPU memory at scale, so a serving system must decide which parts of the cache to keep resident, compress, or evict. The dominant response decides each head’s treatment once, offline or at prefill, and holds that decision fixed for the rest of generation. Existing approaches split along two axes: when a head’s role is decided, and whether a demoted head’s state can be recovered. Static head-role methods (DuoAttention [ 7 ] , RazorAttention [ 8 ] , MoA [ 9 ] , HeadKV [ 10 ] , FlexiCache [ 2 ] , HeteroCache [ 3 ] ) and adaptive allocators (Ada-KV [ 11 ] , CAKE [ 12 ] , LAVa [ 13 ] , DynamicKV [ 14 ] ) both fix treatment offline or at prefill; the adaptive allocators do so despite being framed as dynamic. Decode-time compressors (R-KV [ 6 ] , G-KV [ 15 ] , ThinKV [ 16 ] , SCOPE [ 17 ] ) update during generation but evict destructively; ReasonAlloc [ 4 ] reallocates per-head budgets online but still destroys KV on demotion. Offload systems (ArkVale [ 18 ] , ShadowKV [ 19 ] , InfiniGen [ 20 ] , HeadInfer [ 21 ] , FlexiCache, HeteroCache) keep demoted KV recoverable but never revisit head priority at runtime. Among the systems we survey, none is both dynamic and reversible at once (Figure 1 a). Recent measurement work on retrieval heads [ 1 ] casts doubt on this shared premise: attention-head importance is non-stationary even within a single generation, and that work names dynamic per-head KV retention as an open direction. We close that gap with WakeKV (§ 3 ), a reactive residency policy that never permanently discards a head’s state, and validate it across five real model/regime combinations at matched memory and budget (§ 5 ). Our contributions include: 1. Measurement: We show that attention-head behavior changes during generation, across three models and three regimes, including two that competing frozen-role methods do not evaluate. 2. Prediction study: We find that inexpensive online signals do not reliably anticipate these changes. 3. WakeKV: We introduce reactive, reversible KV residency and show consistent gains over frozen classification, destructive eviction, and three cited baselines, at matched memory or budget. 4. System evaluation: On A30/Mistral-7B via a FlexiCache/vLLM shim, WakeKV reactive beats stock throughput at every rerank interval ( 1.34 1.34 – 2.33 × 2.33	imes ) while holding 95 95 – 99 % 99\% of LongBench quality, confirming the simulator-level direction on real hardware. 2 Motivation Existing KV-cache systems often assume that an attention head’s role remains stable during generation. We ask whether heads instead change behavior over time, and whether those changes can be predicted well enough to prefetch their KV state; § 4 describes the experimental setup. 2.1 Head Churn We first measure how much the set of positions attended to by each head changes from one decoding step to the next. Let A t A_{t} denote the set of heads (or top- k k pages) attended to at decode step t t ; we measure step-to-step stability using the adjacent-step Jaccard index: J ⁡ ( A t , A t + 1 ) = | A t ∩ A t + 1 | | A t ∪ A t + 1 | . The fraction of heads with ≥ 1 \geq 1 HeteroCache-style drift event (windowed-median overlap dropping below τ = 0.5 	au{=}0.5 , baseline reset after each event) ranges 0.63 0.63 – 0.85 0.85 across regimes and holds at 8B ( 0.79 0.79 on CoT). These two numbers describe different things: only 2 2 – 9 % 9\% of heads are persistently unstable (mean RCO below threshold throughout), while 63 63 – 85 % 85\% experience at least one discrete drift event—a small chronically-unstable tail alongside a large majority of occasionally-shifting heads. 2.2 Wake-up Prediction We grade four candidate signals (page-overlap change, windowed-median drift, entropy trend, needle-mass delta) under a causal per-head z-score, z t = ( x t − μ t − w : t ) / σ t − w : t z_{t}=(x_{t}-\mu_{t-w:t})/\sigma_{t-w:t} , computed online from only the trailing w = 32 w{=}32 -step window’s mean and standard deviation. The best signal achieves precision 0.08 0.08 – 0.20 0.20 at recall 0.41 0.41 – 0.70 0.70 (an ensemble never beats the single best). A structurally different candidate—whether the just-generated token predicts a wake burst (Bonferroni-corrected, held out)—reaches F1 0.53 0.53 – 0.62 0.62 on CoT, 4 4 – 5 × 5	imes every attention-derived signal, but zero markers survive on NIAH/multi-turn. Wake-ups are also bursty ( z = + 9.7 z=+9.7 vs. shuffle null), so a coarse trigger only catches 54% of them at a 2%-of-steps rate. Neither cheap proactive route proved reliable enough to prefetch on in our experiments. Together, these findings motivate WakeKV (§ 3 ): heads shift too much for a one-time classification, but not predictably enough to prefetch—so WakeKV reacts to demand instead of anticipating it. 3 Method WakeKV replaces per-head classification with a single runtime rule: each head keeps a GPU-resident set, LRU-ordered and capped at a per-head budget B B ; an evicted page is demoted to a CPU reservoir rather than destroyed, and is fetched back the moment it is wanted again (Figure 1 b). A wrong or stale classification thus costs one recoverable stall, not a permanent accuracy loss. Concretely, each head maintains a GPU-resident set ordered by recency, a CPU reservoir holding every demoted page’s full, uncompressed key/value state, and a budget B B capping GPU residency. Each step’s attention over resident pages defines demand : read pages move to the front of the LRU order. When demand pushes the resident set past B B , the least-recently-used page is demoted —copied to the reservoir, not discarded. A later want of a non-resident page is a miss : its exact state is fetched back before that step’s attention completes, at the cost of one PCIe transfer, with nothing about its history lost. This single rule both narrows a head’s working set (via B B ) and restores it on demand (via fetch) without ever committing to a permanent classification. offline/prefill dynamic/runtime Reversible FlexiCache HeteroCache Reversible WakeKV (this paper) closes the gap Destructive DuoAttention, HeadKV, Ada-KV, CAKE, +4 more Destructive R-KV, SCOPE, ThinKV, ReasonAlloc (a) Method landscape by the two axes GPU resident (per-head LRU, budget B B ) CPU reservoir (recoverable) ∅ \varnothing destroyed (unrecoverable) demote: over budget (LRU) fetch: miss, wanted again evict (foil) (b) WakeKV’s reactive residency mechanism Figure 1: (a) Prior methods split along two axes—when role is decided, and whether demotion is reversible—leaving the dynamic-and-reversible quadrant empty until WakeKV. (b) A demoted head’s state moves to a recoverable CPU reservoir instead of being destroyed; the evict foil (dashed) shares WakeKV’s exact LRU schedule but destroys state instead of reserving it. 4 Evaluation Setup We evaluate on three models, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, across three regimes: NIAH (needle retrieval, ≈ \approx 5000-token filler), long CoT (MATH-500 [ 22 ] , up to 2048 generated tokens), and multi-turn recall. At every decode step and head we log the top- k k attended positions and weights ( k = 64 k=64 ), along with a continuous needle score and a binary copy-paste score following [ 1 ] ’s Eq. 1–2. The 1.5B and 3B models were measured on an RTX 2080 Ti (11GB); the 8B model and the real-system follow-up ran on an A30 (24GB). These logs support the analyses in § 2 and § 5 (which adds a fifth combo, Mistral-7B/NIAH); the real-hardware deployment runs live on a separate A30. 5 Results Having established that heads shift substantially and cheap prediction cannot reliably anticipate wake events (§ 2 ), we ask whether reacting to demand pays off: we simulate WakeKV against a frozen classifier and a destructive-eviction foil sharing its exact LRU schedule, then extend to three baselines and a real-hardware deployment. Because two policies at the same nominal budget can realize different memory, every comparison below holds memory or budget fixed rather than a shared label. Sweeping budget B B traces each policy’s (memory, miss-rate) curve (Figure 2 ); since frozen and reactive reach different memory at the same B B , we interpolate reactive’s curve onto frozen’s 17 measured memory values (pooled across combos, dropping 3 of 20 points that reactive never reached). At those 17 matched-memory levels, reactive’s miss rate is ≤ \leq frozen’s: 17/17 . At matched budget (no interpolation needed), reactive beats evict in 19/20 settings; the sole exception, at the tightest 8B/CoT budget, is where recovering a page that evict would have destroyed alters the subsequent resident set. Figure 2: Memory-vs-miss-rate Pareto fronts across NIAH, CoT, and multi-turn. Reactive sits at or below frozen’s at all 17 matched-memory points and below evict’s at 19 of 20 matched budgets (Table 1 ). We further compare against simulator-compatible reimplementations of three cited methods—SnapKV [ 5 ] , uniform R-KV [ 6 ] , and ReasonAlloc [ 4 ] (each a declared simplification; details in Appendix A )—at matched rather than nominal memory, since all three prune periodically and can use several times reactive’s memory at the same B B (Table 3 , “Reactive mem”). Reactive wins 32/32 comparisons across the four eligible combos—e.g. on 8B/CoT at ∼ \sim 28k pages of realized memory, R-KV’s miss rate is 0.132 0.132 against reactive’s 0.078 0.078 (Table 1 † ). 5.2 Real-Hardware Deployment A FlexiCache/vLLM shim turns stock FlexiCache into WakeKV reactive: zero heads classified “stable,” reranking every step instead of its native cadence. The strict reactive configuration (rerank every step, R = 1 R{=}1 ) is WakeKV’s design point, beating stock throughput by 1.34 × 1.34	imes at 97.4 % 97.4\% LongBench quality. Relaxing how often WakeKV rechecks head residency trades strictness for throughput, tracing a frontier that reaches 2.33 × 2.33	imes at R = 16 R{=}16 while quality stays above 95 % 95\% (Table 2 ). Bold marks speedup over stock; R = 1 R{=}1 is WakeKV’s design point, ⋆ R = 16 R{=}16 its Pareto knee (quality stays above 95 % 95\% ). 6 Conclusion and Future Work Head importance need not be classified once and frozen. A single reactive rule—demote under pressure, fetch on demand, never discard—consistently beats both the frozen and destructive alternatives (Table 1 ), and the gain carries from simulation through to real hardware. Several limitations remain: our evaluation is limited to 1.5B–8B models with uneven regime coverage; the simulator counts misses , not stall time , against FlexiCache- style policies rather than exact code; and the real-system result is narrow (one model/regime, one A30). A natural next step is comparing reversible and destructive eviction on a real system using stall time. Still, reactive, reversible residency is a promising alternative to fixed per-head classification.
